questions.q: What is the narrative point of view used in "fcLdksgj dh ekVh", and who is the protagonist?
questions.a: The memoir is written in first-person point of view ("I" narrator), and the protagonist is the narrator himself — the author Prabha Khaitan reflecting on her childhood. A wrong answer (e.g., "third person" or "the mother is the protagonist") reveals confusion between the title character and the narrative voice, a common error when the title names a supporting character.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the narrator's relationship with his mother changes from the opening scenes to the end of the memoir.
questions.a: Initially, the narrator is entirely dependent on his mother for physical comfort (sleeping on her lap, being fed) and emotional security; later, he becomes her caretaker during her illness, and finally, after her death, he internalizes her presence as a guiding memory. A wrong answer that describes the relationship as static shows inability to track character development across time.

questions.q: Find two passages where the narrator reveals his sensitivity to nature. For each, state the specific sensory detail he notices and what it tells us about his temperament.
questions.a: Example 1: The monsoon arrival — he notices the smell of wet earth, the sound of frogs, the green darkness — showing acute sensory awareness. Example 2: The description of the "iwQy" (seasons) through village sounds and bird calls — showing poetic attunement to cycles. A wrong answer that only lists "he likes nature" without textual evidence reveals surface-level reading.

questions.q: Compare the narrator's childhood fear of the dark (described in the middle sections) with his adult reflection on mortality after his mother's death. What does this comparison reveal about his psychological growth?
questions.a: Childhood fear is concrete and external (ghosts, shadows, needing mother's presence); adult reflection is abstract and internal (accepting impermanence, finding continuity in memory). The shift shows movement from dependence to self-reliance, from sensory fear to philosophical acceptance. A wrong answer that treats both fears as identical misses the developmental arc.

questions.q: Critique the view that the narrator is merely a passive recorder of village life. Use at least two scenes where his active choices shape the narrative.
questions.a: The narrator actively chooses to: (1) sneak out to watch the monsoon despite fear, showing curiosity overriding caution; (2) create a secret language with his mother, showing agency in bonding; (3) decide to stay by his dying mother instead of fleeing grief. These are not passive observations — they are deliberate acts that define his character. A wrong answer claiming passivity ignores the memoir's focus on subjective experience.

questions.q: Write a 100-word diary entry from the narrator's perspective on the night of his mother's funeral, capturing his voice, vocabulary, and emotional state as established in the text.
questions.a: A strong entry uses first-person, present-tense sensory details (smell of incense, sound of wind), references their private rituals (the secret language, the lap-sleeping), and ends with a resolve to carry her memory — not just sadness. A weak entry uses generic grief language ("I miss her so much") without textual anchoring, showing failure to internalize the narrator's unique voice.
